Good job, CGP Grey! I’ve been a hospital based psychiatrist for the past 35 years. In 2024, I saw my first patient who had been supplementing his M.D. appointments with a AI “counselor”. He lived in a rural area where access to in-person counseling was difficult to schedule. It helped him to practice/ use relaxation skills. 10 years today since this video, let's check in on the data: US Unemployment Rate 2014: 5.6% 2024: 4.3% (lower) US Labor Force Participation 2014: 62.2% 2024: 61.9% (slightly lower, but mostly due to the pandemic. The rate is actually increasing) US Population 2014: 321 million 2024: 341 million (~20 million more people) Put another way, in the US alone, there are now 23 million more jobs being done by people in 2024 then there were in 2014. And since full employment is typically assumed to be no lower than ~4%, the short version is that pretty much every human in the US who wants a job has got a job. Regardless of how compelling this video is or how illustrative its story telling, the conclusion it comes to about the impact of AI on jobs is simply not substantiated by the data. The data over the last decade says that AI does... not... take... jobs. Even though this time may have really felt different, it wasn't different. And no, the AI boom marked by the release of ChatGPT and its cohort doesn't change the conclusion. That boom is ~2 years old now. The unemployment rate is flat, and the LFPR is increasing. If AI has automated jobs away in the last 2 years without replacing them, then it hasn't shown up in the data. I love Grey's work, but this video was a miss. The numbers here just don't match up with the story. Regardless of how much it seems like the AI takeover is iminent... Regarless of how compelling analogies about horses are... Regardless of how remarkable and powerful AI is... Regardless of how big of an effect AI and automation has had and will continue to have on civilization... The data is simply undeniable: The advance of automation has not (and is not) reducing the number of jobs available for humans to do. Humans very much need to apply.

I have one issue with this video, the suggestion that teachers and nurses would be easier to replace with AI then computer programmers. The bulk of work I do as a teacher is not relaying information to a child so that they can regurgitate it to me. That's what the school board would *like* me to be. The bulk of my work is spending many hours making human connections with my students and their parents and working with them to ensure the student learns as much as they can. And it's my form belief that those kinds of jobs, teachers and nurses, *high skill* baristas and bartenders etc. Will be the last jobs to be replaced, maybe never be replaced. Much like there are horses still employed today, either in very specific useful ways or in very showy ways. The pony tracks are still a thing, NYPD still has horse back officers. There will *be* jobs useful for humans to be in and I think it will be ones where that kind of human connection is required.

This video is too relevant to the point of being even more discomforting than when it was uploaded. But... why worry? Maybe it’s just my near-unwavering optimism that I try to keep up, but even if large corporate entities would rather purchase AI than hire employees, even if there’s really no job robots won’t be able to replicate, won’t there always be people that prefer to work with other people? Even if a robot is more precise, a human is more sociable Even if a robot costs less, a human is more interactive Even if a robot can replicate these two things, won’t some or even most still see it as more flat or unnerving than if they just hired someone like that? Even if larger corporation which control the economy are automating, the local supplementary businesses that don’t are still necessary for the economy to thrive. Besides, most people either prefer working with people or working alone, then they’re either able to interact with others which the human psyche needs, or they don’t have to worry about others meddling with their affairs. There may be less positions, and we may go through another depression, but even if economic worst comes to fruition, the least people can do is realize the mistake of trusting robots more than people, who need jobs to keep the economy flowing. Robots aren’t evil, no, but automation is both bad and inevitable, not just inevitable. So really, in the depression speculated to be surfacing sometime in the future, I wish people just ask to themselves Was it worth it?

The one problem with this whole concept is liability. In a legal sense, if a bot makes a mistake that harms or even kills somebody, the creator of that bot is legally liable and has to take steps to make sure it doesn't happen again. If a human kills somebody, that's just one person copping the blame for it, and it only affects the job that one person performs. Take Watson, one bot using the same code to treat many patients. If Watson gives the wrong medical treatment, it potentially has to be shut down while the issue is investigated and resolved. For this duration of time, all of Watson's patients (which could number very high if there's only a few functional medical bots that have replaced thousands of medical professionals) get left untreated. Watson could be an order of magnitude better than a system of human professionals but it presents a much greater risk to the integrity of the whole sector and will never be perfect. This risk is obviously diluted by having a larger selection of bots doing the same job, but each bot needs at least a few people overseeing it or being able to engage with it if something goes wrong. Keeping in mind that the whole reason to switch to a bot is to spend less money on human employees, in order for the decision to be viable financially, bots must necessarily take on a greater work load than a human in the same profession. Given how little the human creators of bots actually know about the function of the bots simply by the mechanism of machine learning, bots might potentially be out of commission for months while issues get resolved or a court case takes place. I think bots are a very useful tool but unless we change our current legal system or the enforcement of laws becomes ineffective somehow, bots are always going to need oversight and be beholden to some sort of human being that can be appealed to if something goes wrong.
